t: Number of Different Integers in a String: Normalize Then Dedupe
o: After conceptually replacing every letter with a space, word shatters into maximal digit runs, each denoting an integer that may carry leading zeros; we must count distinct numeric values, treating 1, 01, and 001 as equal. Example 3 (a1b01c001) produces runs 1, 01, 001 which all normalize to the same value, so the answer is 1; Example 1 yields runs 123, 34, 8, 34 with the duplicate 34 collapsing, so the answer is 3; Example 2 yields 1234 and 234 for an answer of 2. The string can reach 1000 characters, so one run may hold a 1000-digit number — parsing into machine integers is unsafe, and the robust move is to compare canonical strings: strip leading zeros while always keeping at least one digit so all-zero runs collapse to 0.
k: Compare normalized decimal strings rather than parsed integers — digit runs may exceed 64-bit range.
Canonical form strips leading zeros but keeps at least one digit, so 000 and 0 both become 0.
Integers are maximal stretches of digits bounded by letters or the string ends — findable in a single two-pointer pass.

a.i: Swap every non-digit for a space, split on whitespace to isolate the runs, canonicalize each token by stripping leading zeros (with a fallback to the single-character 0), and collect results in a set. Regex and split primitives do the tokenizing for you, making this the shortest faithful implementation.
s: Replace every character outside 0-9 with a space.
Split on spaces and skip empty tokens.
Strip leading zeros from each token, substituting 0 if nothing remains.
Insert canonical tokens into a set and return its size.
a.t: O(L) — each character is rewritten once, each token normalized once, with hashing proportional to token length.
a.sp: O(L) — the set stores canonical copies of the extracted runs.

a.i: Walk the string once with index i. When word[i] is not a digit, advance; otherwise extend a second pointer j to the end of the digit run, then a third position k past any leading zeros while keeping at least one character, and insert substring word[k..j) into the set before jumping i to j. No regex machinery, predictable memory, and identical asymptotics — often preferred in C++ or when interviewers ask to avoid built-in splitting.
s: Scan i left to right, skipping non-digit characters.
On entering a run, advance j until the first non-digit after i.
Advance k from i past leading zeros but never past j - 1, preserving a single final digit for all-zero runs.
Add word[k..j) to the set and continue scanning from j.
a.t: O(L) — every character is visited a constant number of times by the three pointers combined.
a.sp: O(L) — canonical substrings retained in the hash set.

w: Either approach passes easily; choose regex-split for brevity in Python or JavaScript and the manual scan in C++ or when asked to avoid library helpers. Pitfalls: parsing tokens into integers (1000-digit overflow), stripping zeros down to an empty string instead of keeping one 0 (000 must equal 0), forgetting that letters fully separate numbers (no sign handling exists here), and miscounting duplicates like the repeated 34 in Example 1. Edge cases worth checking: strings with no digits at all (answer 0), a single all-zero run, and digits glued across multiple letter groups. Follow-up: report the distinct values themselves in numeric order, which invites storing canonical forms keyed by (length, lexicographic) comparison.
